questions.stem: The community health nurse is planning a health promotion program for older adults at a senior center. Which topic should the nurse prioritize based on the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in this population?

options.text: Sexually transmitted infection prevention
Fall prevention and home safety
Childhood immunization schedules
Sports injury prevention

rationales.whyCorrect: Falls are the leading cause of injury-related morbidity and mortality among older adults. Fall prevention and home safety directly address this significant risk. While other topics have value, prioritizing the highest-incidence risk factor is the correct public health nursing approach.
rationales.eli10: Older adults are more likely to fall than any other age group. Falls can break bones and cause serious injuries. Teaching about fall prevention helps keep older adults safe at home. A nurse's job is to focus on the biggest risk first.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of adolescents about healthy lifestyle choices. Which statement by a participant indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I should wear a helmet when I ride my bike."
"Vaping is a safe alternative to smoking cigarettes."
"Eating breakfast every morning helps me focus at school."
"I try to get at least 60 minutes of physical activity each day."

rationales.whyCorrect: Vaping is not a safe alternative to smoking. E-cigarettes contain nicotine and other harmful chemicals that can damage developing brains and lungs. This statement reflects a common misconception among adolescents and requires correction.
rationales.eli10: Many teens think vaping is safe, but it is not. Vapes still have nicotine, which is addictive. Nicotine can hurt a growing brain. A nurse should correct this wrong belief right away.

questions.stem: The school nurse is assessing a 7-year-old child. Which finding is consistent with expected growth and development for this age?

options.text: Ability to think abstractly about hypothetical situations
Preference for solitary play over group activities
Development of logical thinking about concrete objects and events
Onset of secondary sexual characteristics

rationales.whyCorrect: According to Piaget, a 7-year-old is in the concrete operational stage. Children at this age can think logically about concrete objects and events but cannot yet reason abstractly. Abstract thinking develops later in adolescence during the formal operational stage.
rationales.eli10: A 7-year-old can solve problems they can see and touch. They understand that if you pour water from a short cup into a tall one, it's still the same amount. But they cannot think about things that are not real or in front of them. That kind of thinking comes later when they are teenagers.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing anticipatory guidance to the parents of a 4-month-old infant. Which statement by a parent indicates understanding of injury prevention?

options.text: "We should place our baby on the stomach to sleep."
"It is safe to leave our baby on the changing table for a moment while I grab a diaper."
"We need to make sure the crib slats are no more than 2 and 3/8 inches apart."
"We can start using a forward-facing car seat now that the baby holds up their head."

rationales.whyCorrect: Crib slats should be no more than 2 and 3/8 inches apart to prevent the infant's head from becoming entrapped. Infants should sleep on their backs (not stomach) to reduce SIDS risk. Infants should never be left unattended on elevated surfaces. Infants should remain in rear-facing car seats until at least age 2.
rationales.eli10: Babies can get their heads stuck if crib bars are too far apart. Always put a baby to sleep on their back, not their tummy. Never leave a baby alone on a high surface like a changing table. Keep babies in rear-facing car seats as long as possible — it protects their neck and spine.

questions.stem: The nurse is conducting a health literacy assessment during a home visit. Which action best evaluates the client's understanding of the medication regimen?

options.text: Asking, "Do you understand how to take your medicine?"
Providing a printed handout with medication instructions
Using the teach-back method: "Can you show me how you would take your pills tomorrow?"
Reviewing the medication labels aloud with the client

rationales.whyCorrect: The teach-back method is the gold standard for assessing health literacy and confirming understanding. Asking the client to demonstrate or explain in their own words reveals whether learning has occurred. Asking "Do you understand?" often elicits a reflexive "yes" even when the client does not comprehend.
rationales.eli10: Instead of asking "Do you understand?" — because most people just say yes — ask the person to show you. Say, "Can you show me how you would take your medicine?" If they can explain or show it, you know they really understand. This is called teach-back.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching an older adult client about a new antihypertensive medication. Which teaching strategy is most appropriate for this age group?

options.text: Providing detailed written information in small font to save paper
Speaking loudly and using medical terminology to ensure accuracy
Using large-print materials, speaking clearly, and allowing extra time for questions
Teaching the client's family member instead of the client

rationales.whyCorrect: Older adults may have sensory changes including reduced vision. Large-print materials, clear speech at a normal volume (not shouting), and extra time for processing accommodate these normal age-related changes. Teaching should be directed to the client unless cognitive impairment prevents understanding.
rationales.eli10: As people get older, their eyesight may not be as sharp. Use big print so they can read it. Speak clearly — you do not need to shout. Give them extra time to ask questions. Always teach the client, not just the family.

questions.stem: The nurse is counseling a 55-year-old client about colorectal cancer screening. The client asks, "Which test should I choose?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You must have a colonoscopy every year."
"There are several options including colonoscopy, fecal immunochemical testing, and stool DNA testing. Let's discuss what might work best for you."
"Colorectal cancer screening is only needed if you have symptoms."
"I recommend you choose the least expensive option."

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiple screening modalities exist for colorectal cancer including colonoscopy, FIT, and stool DNA testing. The nurse should present evidence-based options and engage in shared decision-making. Screening is recommended for average-risk adults starting at age 45, not only when symptoms appear.
rationales.eli10: There is more than one way to screen for colon cancer. A colonoscopy uses a camera. A FIT test checks for hidden blood in stool. The nurse should explain the choices and help the client decide. Shared decision-making means the client and nurse work together to choose.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an 18-month-old toddler during a well-child visit. Which gross motor skill should the nurse expect?

options.text: Riding a tricycle
Walking up and down stairs with assistance
Skipping and hopping on one foot
Standing on tiptoes for extended periods

rationales.whyCorrect: At 18 months, a toddler can typically walk up and down stairs with assistance (holding a hand or railing). Riding a tricycle is a 3-year-old skill. Skipping and hopping on one foot develop around age 4 to 5. Standing on tiptoes briefly may be seen, but extended periods are not expected.
rationales.eli10: An 18-month-old is learning to walk better. They can walk up and down stairs if someone holds their hand. Riding a tricycle comes later, around age 3. Skipping and hopping come even later, around age 4 or 5.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing nutrition education to a client with a body mass index of 32 kg/m². Which statement reflects the best approach?

options.text: "You need to stop eating all carbohydrates immediately."
"Let's talk about small, realistic changes you can make to your eating and activity habits."
"Obesity is mostly genetic, so there is not much you can do."
"You should join a weight-loss program and lose 50 pounds in the next two months."

rationales.whyCorrect: A BMI of 32 kg/m² falls in the obesity range. The best approach is motivational interviewing and collaborative goal-setting focused on small, sustainable lifestyle changes. Extreme, rapid, or overly restrictive recommendations are neither safe nor sustainable.
rationales.eli10: Telling someone to make huge changes all at once usually does not work. Small changes are easier to stick with. The nurse should ask what small change the client feels ready to try. Maybe a 10-minute walk or swapping soda for water. These small steps add up over time.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about influenza vaccination. The client states, "I'm healthy and never get the flu. I don't need the vaccine." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "You are right. Healthy people do not need the flu shot."
"The flu shot is required by law for all adults."
"Even healthy people can get seriously ill from influenza, and vaccination helps protect others who may be more vulnerable."
"If you change your mind, the vaccine is only available in the fall."

rationales.whyCorrect: Even healthy individuals can develop severe influenza and complications. Vaccination provides individual protection and contributes to herd immunity, protecting vulnerable populations such as infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. The vaccine is not legally mandated for all adults.
rationales.eli10: Even healthy people can get very sick from the flu. Getting the flu shot also protects people around you — like babies, older relatives, and people with weak immune systems. It is like putting on a seatbelt. You hope you never need it, but it can save your life.

questions.stem: The nurse is performing a developmental screening on a 3-year-old child. Which behavior is most concerning and warrants further evaluation?

options.text: The child engages in parallel play alongside other children
The child uses two- to three-word sentences
The child has no interest in interacting with caregivers and does not respond to their name
The child insists on the same bedtime routine every night

rationales.whyCorrect: A 3-year-old who shows no interest in caregivers and does not respond to their name raises concern for autism spectrum disorder. Parallel play, two- to three-word sentences, and insistence on routines are developmentally appropriate for this age.
rationales.eli10: A 3-year-old should want to interact with parents and respond when called by name. If a child ignores people and does not respond to their name, it could be a sign of a developmental problem. The nurse should flag this for further checking. Wanting the same routine and playing next to (but not with) other kids is normal at this age.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing discharge teaching to a client who speaks limited English. An interpreter is not immediately available. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Use a family member who speaks both languages to translate
Speak slowly and loudly in English, using hand gestures
Wait for a qualified medical interpreter to become available
Provide written discharge instructions in English for the client to translate at home

rationales.whyCorrect: Professional medical interpreters ensure accurate communication and protect client safety. Using family members can lead to errors in translation, breach of confidentiality, and role confusion. The nurse should wait for a qualified interpreter rather than use informal or written methods that could compromise understanding and safety.
rationales.eli10: A family member might not translate medical words correctly. They might also change what is said or leave things out. A trained medical interpreter knows the right words and keeps things private. It is safer to wait for a professional interpreter.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an infant at a 9-month well-child visit. Which finding is expected for this age?

options.text: Walks independently across the room
Displays stranger anxiety and clings to parent
Stacks four to six blocks into a tower
Speaks in two-word phrases

rationales.whyCorrect: Stranger anxiety typically emerges around 8 to 9 months and is a normal developmental milestone indicating healthy attachment. Walking independently is a 12-month skill. Stacking blocks and two-word phrases develop later.
rationales.eli10: Around 9 months old, babies start to fear strangers. They cling to their parent when someone new comes near. This is actually a good sign — it means the baby has a healthy bond with their caregiver. It is totally normal and expected.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about secondary prevention. Which intervention is an example of secondary prevention?

options.text: Administering the hepatitis B vaccine to a newborn
Teaching a client with diabetes how to perform foot care
Performing a mammogram to screen for breast cancer
Referring a client to cardiac rehabilitation after a myocardial infarction

rationales.whyCorrect: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and screening. Mammography screens for breast cancer before symptoms appear. Vaccination is primary prevention. Teaching foot care and cardiac rehabilitation are tertiary prevention (managing established disease).
rationales.eli10: Primary prevention stops a disease before it starts — like vaccines. Secondary prevention finds a disease early — like mammograms that look for breast cancer before you can feel it. Tertiary prevention helps manage a disease you already have — like teaching foot care to someone with diabetes.

questions.stem: The nurse is counseling parents about car seat safety for their 2-year-old child who weighs 28 pounds. Which recommendation is correct?

options.text: Use a forward-facing car seat in the front passenger seat
Use a rear-facing car seat in the back seat
Use a booster seat with the vehicle's lap belt only
The child can use the regular seat belt without a booster

rationales.whyCorrect: A 2-year-old weighing 28 pounds should remain in a rear-facing car seat in the back seat. Best practice recommendations are to keep children rear-facing until at least age 2 or until they exceed the seat's height and weight limits. The back seat is the safest location.
rationales.eli10: Keep toddlers in rear-facing car seats as long as possible. In a crash, a rear-facing seat protects the child's head, neck, and spine. Always put the car seat in the back seat. The front seat has airbags that can hurt a child.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning a community health fair. Which screening should the nurse include for adults aged 45 and older according to current preventive guidelines?

options.text: Routine scoliosis screening
Colorectal cancer screening
Newborn metabolic screening
School-entry vision screening

rationales.whyCorrect: Colorectal cancer screening is recommended for average-risk adults starting at age 45. Scoliosis screening is for school-age children. Newborn metabolic screening is for infants. School-entry vision screening is for young children.
rationales.eli10: Once adults turn 45, they should start getting checked for colon cancer. This screening can find problems early when they are easier to treat. The other screenings listed are for kids, not adults.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 6-month-old infant. The parent reports, "My baby was born at 32 weeks." When evaluating developmental milestones, the nurse should:

options.text: Use the infant's chronological age of 6 months
Use the infant's adjusted age of 4 months
Expect the infant to have caught up and use chronological age
Refer the infant immediately to early intervention regardless of findings

rationales.whyCorrect: For preterm infants, adjusted age (chronological age minus weeks born early) should be used for developmental assessment until at least age 2. A 6-month-old born at 32 weeks has an adjusted age of approximately 4 months. Using chronological age would mislabel the infant as delayed.
rationales.eli10: When a baby is born early, you cannot expect them to hit milestones at the same time as a full-term baby. Subtract the weeks they came early from their actual age. That gives you their "adjusted age." A baby born 8 weeks early who is now 6 months old should act like a 4-month-old.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of older adults about maintaining cognitive health. Which recommendation is supported by evidence?

options.text: "Avoid all mental challenges to prevent overexertion."
"Engage in regular physical activity, social interaction, and mentally stimulating activities."
"Take high-dose vitamin E supplements to prevent memory loss."
"Cognitive decline is inevitable and cannot be slowed."

rationales.whyCorrect: Evidence supports that physical activity, social engagement, and cognitive stimulation help maintain cognitive function in older adults. Cognitive decline is not inevitable. High-dose vitamin E has not been proven to prevent cognitive decline and can have risks.
rationales.eli10: Staying active — physically, socially, and mentally — helps keep the brain healthy as people age. Walking, talking with friends, reading, doing puzzles — all of these help. Losing memory is not something that has to happen to everyone. The brain is like a muscle: use it or lose it.

questions.stem: The nurse is conducting a health history with an adolescent. Which approach best promotes open communication?

options.text: Asking the parent to remain in the room during the entire interview
Asking direct, rapid-fire questions about sensitive topics
Interviewing the adolescent alone for part of the visit and explaining confidentiality limits
Avoiding topics related to sexual health and substance use

rationales.whyCorrect: Adolescents are more likely to disclose sensitive information when interviewed alone. The nurse should explain confidentiality while also clarifying its limits (safety concerns requiring disclosure). Having the parent present for the entire interview inhibits honest communication.
rationales.eli10: Teens will talk more honestly about private things when their parent is not in the room. The nurse should spend part of the visit talking to the teen alone. But the nurse must also explain: "What you tell me is private unless I am worried about your safety." This builds trust.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing education about hypertension prevention to a group of African American adults. Which dietary teaching is most culturally sensitive and evidence-based?

options.text: "Stop eating all traditional foods immediately."
"Consider reducing sodium intake by using herbs and spices for seasoning instead of salt."
"Hypertension is genetic, so dietary changes will not help."
"You only need to worry about blood pressure if you feel symptoms."

rationales.whyCorrect: African American adults have higher rates of hypertension. A culturally sensitive approach acknowledges dietary traditions while suggesting practical modifications — such as seasoning with herbs and spices instead of salt. Framing it as an addition (trying new flavors) rather than a restriction improves adherence.
rationales.eli10: Instead of saying "stop eating your cultural foods," the nurse should find ways to make traditional foods healthier. Suggest using garlic, onion, lemon, and herbs for flavor instead of salt. This respects the person's culture while helping them get healthier.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 5-year-old child for school readiness. Which skill indicates readiness for kindergarten?

options.text: Ability to read chapter books independently
Ability to count to 10, recognize some letters, and follow two-step directions
Ability to solve algebraic equations
Complete independence in all self-care activities without reminders

rationales.whyCorrect: Kindergarten readiness includes counting to 10, recognizing some letters, following simple directions, and basic social skills like sharing. Reading chapter books and solving algebra are far beyond typical 5-year-old skills. Complete independence is not expected.
rationales.eli10: A 5-year-old getting ready for kindergarten should be able to count to 10, know some letters, and follow simple two-step directions like "hang up your coat and sit on the mat." They do not need to read chapter books or do math. That comes later.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing teaching about skin cancer prevention. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I only need sunscreen when I go to the beach."
"A tanning bed is safer than the sun for getting a tan."
"I should use a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply every two hours."
"People with darker skin do not need to worry about skin cancer."

rationales.whyCorrect: Broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, reapplied every two hours (and after swimming or sweating), is the evidence-based recommendation for skin cancer prevention. Tanning beds emit UV radiation and increase cancer risk. All skin tones are at risk.
rationales.eli10: Sunscreen is not just for the beach. Use it every day on skin that is not covered by clothes. SPF 30 or higher works best. Put it on again every two hours. Tanning beds are not safe — they damage skin just like the sun. Everyone, with any skin color, needs sun protection.

questions.stem: The school nurse notices that a 10-year-old child's BMI is above the 95th percentile for age and sex. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Tell the child to go on a strict diet immediately
Recommend that the child be evaluated by a healthcare provider for further assessment and support
Ignore the finding since children often outgrow weight issues
Send a letter home stating the child is obese

rationales.whyCorrect: A BMI above the 95th percentile indicates obesity. The priority is recommending further evaluation by a healthcare provider who can assess for comorbidities and provide comprehensive management. The nurse should communicate sensitively and avoid stigmatizing language.
rationales.eli10: The nurse should not ignore a high BMI or use hurtful labels. Instead, recommend that the child see a doctor who can check for related health problems and help the family make a plan. The goal is to help, not to shame.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning a smoking cessation program for a community. Which approach is most effective for primary prevention?

options.text: Providing low-dose CT scans for early lung cancer detection
Offering nicotine replacement therapy and counseling to current smokers
Implementing school-based education programs to prevent smoking initiation
Referring smokers with emphysema to pulmonary rehabilitation

rationales.whyCorrect: Primary prevention prevents disease from occurring. School-based education programs that prevent smoking initiation are primary prevention. Low-dose CT scans are secondary (screening). Nicotine replacement for current smokers and pulmonary rehab for emphysema are tertiary.
rationales.eli10: Primary prevention stops a problem before it starts. Teaching kids in school about the dangers of smoking — before they ever try it — is primary prevention. Screening tests and treating people who already smoke are different levels of prevention. They are important, but they happen after the risk already exists.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching an older adult client about preventing constipation. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: "Avoid all fiber in your diet."
"Increase your fluid intake, eat high-fiber foods, and stay physically active."
"Take a stimulant laxative every day to prevent constipation."
"Limit fluid intake to reduce the need for bathroom trips."

rationales.whyCorrect: Constipation prevention in older adults includes adequate fluid intake, dietary fiber, and physical activity. Stimulant laxatives can cause dependence and electrolyte imbalances if used daily. Limiting fluids can worsen constipation.
rationales.eli10: Older adults sometimes get constipated because they do not drink enough water, eat enough fiber, or move around enough. Drinking more water, eating fruits and vegetables, and going for walks can all help. Taking laxatives every day is not safe — the body can become dependent on them.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a 2-month-old infant during a well-child visit. Which finding requires immediate intervention?

options.text: The infant's posterior fontanelle is closed
The infant does not smile in response to the parent's face
The infant startles and extends the arms when exposed to a loud noise
The infant's weight has doubled since birth

rationales.whyCorrect: A social smile in response to a caregiver's face typically develops by 6 to 8 weeks. Absence of this social smile at 2 months may indicate a developmental or attachment concern. Posterior fontanelle closure at 2 months is normal. Startle (Moro) reflex is expected. Weight doubling by 4 to 6 months is normal — at 2 months, weight may not have doubled yet, but this alone is not the most concerning finding.
rationales.eli10: By 2 months old, a baby should smile back when someone smiles at them. If they do not, the nurse needs to check more carefully. It could be a sign of a developmental delay. The other findings — like startling at loud noises — are normal for a 2-month-old.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes about foot care. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will inspect my feet every day for cuts or blisters."
"I should wear well-fitting shoes and avoid going barefoot."
"I can soak my feet in hot water every night to relax."
"I will report any redness or sores on my feet to my healthcare provider."

rationales.whyCorrect: Clients with diabetes should avoid soaking their feet in hot water due to decreased sensation and risk of burns. They may not feel the water is too hot. Daily inspection, proper footwear, avoiding barefoot walking, and reporting problems are all correct foot care practices.
rationales.eli10: Diabetes can make feet less sensitive to heat and pain. A person with diabetes might soak their feet in hot water and burn themselves without realizing it. Check feet every day, wear shoes that fit well, and never go barefoot. Tell the doctor about any cuts or red spots right away.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing anticipatory guidance to the parents of a 12-month-old. Which statement by a parent indicates understanding of safety?

options.text: "We can turn the car seat forward-facing now that our baby is one year old."
"It is okay to leave small objects on the floor since our baby is not walking yet."
"We have installed safety gates at the top and bottom of the stairs."
"Our baby can sleep with a pillow and heavy blanket now."

rationales.whyCorrect: Safety gates at stairs prevent falls — a leading cause of injury in toddlers. Children should remain rear-facing as long as possible (past age 1). Small objects pose a choking hazard regardless of walking ability. Infants should sleep without pillows or heavy blankets to reduce SIDS risk.
rationales.eli10: A 1-year-old is moving around and can fall down stairs. Safety gates at the top and bottom of stairs are very important. Keep the baby rear-facing in the car seat. No pillows or heavy blankets in the crib — they can cause suffocation. Pick up small objects from the floor — babies put everything in their mouths.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. The client asks, "Why should my 11-year-old child get this vaccine?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "The vaccine is required for school entry."
"The HPV vaccine is most effective when given before exposure to the virus, and it prevents several types of cancer."
"The vaccine only works if given before a child turns 12."
"Your child does not need it if they plan to be abstinent."

rationales.whyCorrect: The HPV vaccine is most effective when given before exposure to the virus, which is why it is recommended at age 11 to 12. It prevents cervical, oropharyngeal, anal, and other HPV-related cancers. It is not required for school entry in all states, and it works best when given before sexual activity begins.
rationales.eli10: The HPV vaccine prevents cancer. It works best if given before a person is ever exposed to HPV. That is why doctors recommend it at age 11 or 12. Even if someone plans to wait to have sex, they should still get the vaccine. It is about cancer prevention.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an older adult client's home environment. Which finding poses the greatest fall risk?

options.text: Grab bars installed in the bathroom
Loose throw rugs on hardwood floors
Night lights in the hallway and bathroom
Handrails on both sides of the staircase

rationales.whyCorrect: Loose throw rugs are a major fall hazard for older adults because they can slip or cause tripping. Grab bars, night lights, and handrails are all fall-prevention measures that increase safety.
rationales.eli10: Throw rugs are dangerous for older adults. They slide around and can trip someone. The best fix is to remove them or use non-slip backing. Grab bars, handrails, and night lights make a home safer — they help prevent falls.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching an adolescent about testicular self-examination. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: "Perform the examination once every two years."
"Perform the examination monthly, after a warm shower, when the scrotum is relaxed."
"Only perform the examination if you feel pain in the testicles."
"Testicular cancer only affects men over age 50, so you do not need to worry now."

rationales.whyCorrect: Testicular self-examination should be performed monthly starting in adolescence. A warm shower relaxes the scrotum, making it easier to palpate the testicles and detect abnormalities. Testicular cancer is most common in young men aged 15 to 35.
rationales.eli10: Young men should check their testicles every month. The best time is after a warm shower when the skin is relaxed. Roll each testicle gently between the fingers to feel for lumps. Testicular cancer happens most often in younger men, not older ones. Finding it early makes it very treatable.

questions.stem: A community health nurse is planning a program to reduce childhood obesity. Which strategy targets the community level of prevention?

options.text: Counseling individual children about calorie counting
Working with schools to increase physical education time and improve cafeteria food options
Prescribing weight-loss medication to children with obesity
Referring children with obesity to endocrinology

rationales.whyCorrect: Community-level interventions target the environment, systems, and policies. Working with schools to change physical education and food options addresses the community level. Individual counseling and referrals target the individual level.
rationales.eli10: Individual interventions help one person at a time. Community interventions change things for everyone at once. Getting schools to offer more gym time and healthier lunches helps every student, not just one. That is community-level prevention.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing anticipatory guidance to the parents of a 15-month-old. Which statement indicates the parents understand nutrition for this age?

options.text: "We can switch our child to skim milk to reduce fat intake."
"Our child should continue drinking whole milk until age two for brain development."
"It is fine to put our child to bed with a bottle of juice."
"Our child needs at least 1,500 calories from solid foods every day."

rationales.whyCorrect: Whole milk is recommended until age 2 because the fat is essential for brain and nervous system development. Skim milk does not provide adequate fat for neurodevelopment. Putting a child to bed with a bottle of juice promotes dental caries.
rationales.eli10: Babies and toddlers need fat for their brains to grow. Whole milk has that fat. After age 2, they can switch to lower-fat milk. Never put a baby to bed with a bottle of milk or juice — it causes cavities.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an older adult client who reports urinary incontinence. Which question is most important for the nurse to ask first?

options.text: "Have you considered wearing adult diapers?"
"When did the incontinence start, and can you describe what happens?"
"Why didn't you mention this problem sooner?"
"Are you limiting your fluid intake to control the issue?"

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse should first assess the nature, onset, and characteristics of the incontinence. Assessment precedes intervention. Asking "why" questions can sound judgmental. Recommending products or assuming fluid restriction comes after a thorough assessment.
rationales.eli10: Before giving advice, the nurse needs to understand the problem. Ask: "When did it start? What exactly happens? Is it a little leak or a lot?" Once you understand, you can help. Do not make the person feel bad by asking "why" in a blaming tone.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about breast self-awareness. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: "If you perform monthly breast self-exams, you do not need mammograms."
"You should become familiar with how your breasts normally look and feel, and report any changes to your healthcare provider."
"Breast cancer always presents as a painful lump."
"Only women with a family history of breast cancer need to be concerned."

rationales.whyCorrect: Current guidelines emphasize breast self-awareness — knowing what is normal for one's own breasts and reporting changes. Mammograms remain important even for those who perform self-exams. Breast cancer does not always present as a painful lump. All women are at risk, not only those with a family history.
rationales.eli10: Every woman should know how her breasts normally look and feel. If something changes — a new lump, dimpling, nipple discharge — tell the doctor. This is called breast self-awareness. It does not replace mammograms. You still need both.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching an older adult client about medication safety. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I can share my medications with my spouse if they have similar symptoms."
"I should keep an updated list of all my medications and bring it to every healthcare visit."
"Herbal supplements do not interact with prescription medications, so I do not need to mention them."
"If I miss a dose, I should double the next dose to catch up."

rationales.whyCorrect: Keeping an updated medication list and bringing it to every visit is a key safety practice. Medications should never be shared. Herbal supplements can interact with prescriptions. Doubling a missed dose can cause dangerous toxicity.
rationales.eli10: Write down every medicine you take — prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, herbs. Bring the list to every doctor visit. Never share medicine with anyone else. Never double up on a missed dose — that can be dangerous. Herbal supplements can affect how prescription medicines work, so always tell your provider about them.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a preschool-aged child. Which behavior represents normal development for a 4-year-old?

options.text: Understanding conservation of volume
Magical thinking and believing that thoughts can cause events
Mastering abstract algebraic reasoning
Demonstrating complete impulse control

rationales.whyCorrect: Magical thinking is characteristic of the preoperational stage (ages 2 to 7). A 4-year-old may believe their thoughts can cause events. Conservation of volume develops later in the concrete operational stage. Abstract reasoning and complete impulse control are not expected at this age.
rationales.eli10: A 4-year-old thinks magically. They might believe that wishing for something makes it happen, or that thinking a bad thought caused something bad. This is normal. They also cannot think abstractly yet or control their impulses fully. That develops as they get older.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health teaching to a client who is newly diagnosed with hypertension. The client says, "I don't feel sick, so why do I need to take medicine?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You're right — if you don't have symptoms, you probably don't need medication."
"Hypertension is often called the 'silent killer' because it damages blood vessels without causing symptoms. Treating it now prevents strokes and heart attacks later."
"Just take the medication and don't question the doctor's orders."
"You can wait until you develop symptoms to start treatment."

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypertension is often asymptomatic while causing progressive vascular damage. Explaining the "silent killer" concept and linking treatment to future stroke and heart attack prevention helps the client understand the rationale. Dismissing the client's concerns or telling them to follow orders without question is not patient-centered care.
rationales.eli10: High blood pressure usually does not make you feel sick. But inside the body, it is quietly damaging blood vessels, the heart, and kidneys. By the time you feel symptoms, a lot of damage may already be done. Taking medicine now prevents strokes and heart attacks later. That is why it is called the silent killer.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a parent about immunizations for a 2-month-old infant. Which vaccines should the nurse include according to the CDC schedule? Select the best answer from the options.

options.text: MMR and varicella
DTaP, IPV, HepB, Hib, PCV13, and rotavirus
HPV and meningococcal conjugate
Tdap booster and influenza only

rationales.whyCorrect: At 2 months, the CDC schedule includes DTaP, IPV, HepB, Hib, PCV13, and rotavirus vaccines. MMR and varicella are given at 12 to 15 months. HPV and meningococcal vaccines are given later in childhood. Tdap is given at age 11 to 12.
rationales.eli10: At 2 months old, babies get several vaccines to protect against serious diseases. These include shots for diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, hepatitis B, and infections that can cause meningitis. They also get a rotavirus vaccine given by mouth. The MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) shot comes later, around the first birthday.

questions.stem: A nurse is conducting a health screening at a community fair. A client has a blood pressure reading of 148/92 mmHg. The client has no history of hypertension. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Tell the client the reading is fine and no follow-up is needed
Recommend the client follow up with a healthcare provider for further evaluation
Diagnose the client with hypertension and recommend medication
Tell the client to restrict all salt immediately and recheck in one year

rationales.whyCorrect: A reading of 148/92 mmHg is elevated and warrants follow-up, but a single reading does not diagnose hypertension. The nurse should recommend the client see a healthcare provider for repeat measurements and evaluation. The nurse cannot diagnose or prescribe.
rationales.eli10: One high blood pressure reading at a health fair does not mean the person has hypertension. It could be stress, caffeine, or just a one-time thing. But it is high enough to need checking. The nurse should say: "This reading is on the high side. Please see your doctor to have it checked again."

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching an older adult client about polypharmacy risks. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will bring all my medications — including over-the-counter drugs — to my next appointment."
"I can take my neighbor's pain medication since it worked well for them."
"I should use one pharmacy for all my prescriptions when possible."
"I will ask my provider to review all my medications at least once a year."

rationales.whyCorrect: Taking another person's medication is dangerous and never appropriate. Medications are prescribed for a specific individual based on their health history, allergies, and other medications. The other statements reflect correct understanding of medication safety practices.
rationales.eli10: Never take someone else's medicine — even if you have similar symptoms. Their medicine was chosen for their body, their health problems, and their other medicines. It could be very dangerous for you. Always use your own prescriptions.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an adolescent for risk-taking behaviors using the HEADSSS framework. Which question best assesses the "Drugs" component?

options.text: "Do you have any friends who use drugs?"
"Do you know drugs are bad for you?"
"Many teens experiment with substances. What has your experience been with alcohol, tobacco, or other drugs?"
"Are your parents aware that teens use drugs?"

rationales.whyCorrect: The HEADSSS assessment uses open-ended, nonjudgmental questions. Normalizing the behavior ("many teens experiment") reduces defensiveness and invites honest disclosure. Asking about friends or parents' awareness is indirect. Telling the teen drugs are "bad" is judgmental.
rationales.eli10: To get honest answers from teens, ask open-ended questions without judging. Say: "Lots of teens try things. What has your experience been?" instead of "Do you use drugs?" The teen is more likely to tell the truth when they do not feel attacked.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about stress management techniques. The client says, "I don't have time to meditate or exercise." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "You will develop serious health problems if you don't manage your stress."
"Even small changes can help — what about a five-minute walk during your lunch break or deep breathing at red lights?"
"Everyone has the same 24 hours. You just need better time management."
"Then there is nothing I can do to help you."

rationales.whyCorrect: Small, realistic stress-management strategies are more achievable than demanding large lifestyle changes. A five-minute walk or deep breathing exercise can be integrated into daily life. Scare tactics, minimizing the client's concern, and abandoning the effort are not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: When someone says they have no time, do not lecture them. Suggest tiny changes that fit into their day. Deep breathing at stoplights. A five-minute walk at lunch. Small moments of calm add up. Help the person find what works in their real life.

questions.stem: A nurse is performing a well-child assessment on a 2-year-old. The parent expresses concern that the child is not yet toilet trained. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Your child should have been toilet trained by 18 months. This is concerning."
"Toilet training readiness varies — many children are not ready until 2 to 3 years of age. Let's talk about signs of readiness."
"Start a strict toilet training regimen immediately."
"Delay toilet training until the child starts kindergarten."

rationales.whyCorrect: Toilet training readiness varies widely, with many children not ready until age 2 to 3. The nurse should educate parents about readiness signs (staying dry for two hours, showing interest, ability to follow simple instructions). Forcing training before readiness can cause frustration for both parent and child.
rationales.eli10: There is no magic age for toilet training. Some kids are ready at 2, some not until 3 or later. Look for signs: the child stays dry for a couple of hours, shows interest in the potty, and can follow simple directions. Do not force it — that only makes everyone stressed.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning a health promotion program for a rural community with limited access to healthcare. Which intervention addresses this barrier most effectively?

options.text: Mailing educational pamphlets to every household
Partnering with a mobile health clinic to provide screenings and vaccinations at community locations
Requiring all residents to travel to the nearest urban hospital for preventive care
Canceling the program because the barrier cannot be overcome

rationales.whyCorrect: Mobile health clinics bring services directly to underserved communities, overcoming transportation and access barriers. Mailing pamphlets does not address the access problem. Requiring travel to urban hospitals maintains the barrier. Canceling the program is not a solution.
rationales.eli10: If people cannot travel to a clinic, bring the clinic to them. Mobile health vans can park at churches, community centers, and schools. This way, people can get check-ups, vaccines, and screenings close to home. It solves the transportation problem.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about the importance of adequate sleep. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: "Adults need at least 9 to 10 hours of sleep per night for optimal health."
"Sleep deprivation is only a concern for people who work night shifts."
"Consistent poor sleep is linked to increased risk of hypertension, obesity, and depression."
"Drinking alcohol before bed improves sleep quality."

rationales.whyCorrect: Chronic sleep deprivation is linked to hypertension, obesity, depression, and impaired immune function. Adults generally need 7 to 9 hours. Sleep deprivation affects anyone, not just night-shift workers. Alcohol disrupts sleep architecture and reduces sleep quality.
rationales.eli10: Not getting enough sleep is bad for your health. It raises the risk of high blood pressure, weight gain, and depression. Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Alcohol before bed might help you fall asleep, but it makes sleep quality worse.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 6-month-old infant's nutrition. The parent reports introducing solid foods. Which food choice is most appropriate for this age?

options.text: Honey-sweetened cereal
Iron-fortified single-grain infant cereal mixed with breast milk or formula
Whole grapes cut into small pieces
Cow's milk in a bottle

rationales.whyCorrect: Iron-fortified single-grain infant cereal is an appropriate first solid food for a 6-month-old. Honey is contraindicated before age 1 due to botulism risk. Whole grapes are a choking hazard. Cow's milk should not be introduced until 12 months.
rationales.eli10: Start solid foods with iron-fortified baby cereal. Mix it with breast milk or formula. Never give honey to a baby under age 1 — it can cause a serious illness called botulism. Whole grapes can choke a baby. Wait until age 1 to give cow's milk.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of middle-aged adults about recommended health screenings. A 50-year-old woman asks which screenings she needs. According to general preventive guidelines, which combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Colorectal cancer screening, mammogram, and blood pressure screening
Newborn metabolic screening and school physical
Only a tetanus booster every 30 years
Prostate cancer screening and testicular examination only

rationales.whyCorrect: For a 50-year-old woman, recommended screenings include colorectal cancer screening (starting at 45), mammography, and blood pressure screening. Newborn screening is for infants. Prostate screening is for men. Tetanus boosters are needed every 10 years, not 30.
rationales.eli10: A 50-year-old woman needs several regular screenings. She should get checked for colon cancer, have mammograms to look for breast cancer, and have her blood pressure checked. These screenings find problems early when they are easiest to treat.

questions.stem: The school nurse is teaching a class about hand hygiene to prevent infection. Which statement by a student indicates understanding?

options.text: "I only need to wash my hands if they look dirty."
"Hand sanitizer works well for all types of germs, including C. difficile."
"I should wash my hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating and after using the bathroom."
"Washing hands with cold water is more effective than using warm water with soap."

rationales.whyCorrect: Handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds is the gold standard for infection prevention. Hand sanitizer does not kill all pathogens (notably C. difficile spores). Hands should be washed before eating, after bathroom use, and whenever visibly soiled — not only when visibly dirty.
rationales.eli10: Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Sing "Happy Birthday" twice. Do this before eating, after the bathroom, and when hands look dirty. Hand sanitizer is good, but it does not kill every germ. Soap and water are still the best.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health teaching to a client who uses complementary and alternative medicine. Which statement by the nurse demonstrates cultural humility?

options.text: "Those treatments are not scientifically proven, so you should stop using them."
"Tell me about the complementary approaches you use so we can ensure they are safe with your prescribed treatments."
"Western medicine is the only effective approach to healthcare."
"I do not need to know about alternative treatments because they do not affect your medical care."

rationales.whyCorrect: Cultural humility involves respectful inquiry about a client's health practices without judgment. Asking what complementary approaches the client uses allows the nurse to assess for interactions with prescribed treatments. Dismissing alternative approaches damages the therapeutic relationship.
rationales.eli10: Many people use herbs, teas, or other treatments along with regular medicine. The nurse should ask about these in a respectful way: "Tell me what else you use for your health." Some herbs can interact with prescription medicines, so it is important to know. Never make a client feel foolish for their health choices.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a pregnant client about nutrition during the first trimester. The client reports nausea and vomiting every morning. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: "Skip breakfast entirely to avoid triggering nausea."
"Eat dry crackers or toast before getting out of bed in the morning."
"Take your prenatal vitamin on an empty stomach first thing in the morning."
"Stop taking prenatal vitamins until the nausea resolves."

rationales.whyCorrect: Eating dry crackers or toast before getting out of bed can help reduce morning nausea by absorbing gastric acid and stabilizing blood sugar. Skipping breakfast can worsen nausea from hypoglycemia. Prenatal vitamins on an empty stomach often increase nausea. Prenatal vitamins should not be stopped without consulting a provider.
rationales.eli10: Morning sickness is common in early pregnancy. Eating a few plain crackers before getting out of bed can help settle the stomach. An empty stomach can actually make nausea worse. Do not stop taking prenatal vitamins — they have important nutrients for the baby.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a postpartum client about warning signs after discharge. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour is normal after delivery."
"I should call my provider if I have a fever over 100.4°F, severe headache, or heavy bleeding."
"Pain and redness in one leg is just normal swelling from delivery."
"I do not need to worry about my mood — feeling sad is just part of being a new mom."

rationales.whyCorrect: Fever over 100.4°F could indicate infection. Severe headache may indicate preeclampsia. Heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour) could indicate hemorrhage. These are all warning signs requiring immediate medical attention. Saturation of a pad in an hour is not normal. Unilateral leg pain with redness may indicate DVT. Mood changes beyond two weeks warrant evaluation.
rationales.eli10: After having a baby, call the doctor if you have a fever, very bad headache, or very heavy bleeding. Soaking through a pad in one hour is too much — that is not normal. Pain and redness in one leg could be a blood clot. Feeling sad is normal for a few days, but if it lasts more than two weeks, get help.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing discharge teaching to a new mother about newborn safety. Which statement by the mother requires follow-up?

options.text: "We will always place the baby on the back to sleep."
"We will keep the room temperature comfortable and avoid overdressing the baby."
"We will place the baby in the car seat on the front passenger seat so we can watch them."
"We will not leave the baby unattended on the changing table."

rationales.whyCorrect: The car seat should be installed in the back seat — never in the front passenger seat where airbags could seriously injure or kill an infant. Back sleeping, appropriate room temperature, and never leaving the baby unattended on elevated surfaces are all correct safety practices.
rationales.eli10: Never put a baby's car seat in the front passenger seat. If the airbag goes off, it can kill or badly hurt the baby. The back seat is always the safest place. Keep the baby on their back to sleep and never leave them alone on a high surface like a changing table.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about contraception options. The client says, "I want a method I don't have to think about every day." Which method best meets this stated need?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill
Male condom
Long-acting reversible contraception such as an intrauterine device or implant
Fertility awareness method

rationales.whyCorrect: Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) such as IUDs and implants provide highly effective contraception for years without requiring daily action. The pill requires daily adherence. Condoms require use with every act of intercourse. Fertility awareness requires daily tracking.
rationales.eli10: If someone wants birth control they do not have to think about every day, an IUD or implant is the best choice. These last for years — no daily pill to remember. The pill must be taken every day. Condoms must be used every time. An IUD or implant is "set it and forget it."

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a client who smokes one pack of cigarettes per day and is considering pregnancy. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "You should quit now — smoking during pregnancy is the worst thing you could do."
"Quitting smoking before pregnancy improves fertility and reduces risks to the baby. Let's talk about resources to help you quit."
"If you cannot quit, just cut down to a few cigarettes a day."
"Smoking only affects the baby in the third trimester, so you have time."

rationales.whyCorrect: Smoking cessation before pregnancy improves fertility and reduces risks including miscarriage, preterm birth, and low birth weight. A supportive, nonjudgmental approach with practical resources is most effective. Scare tactics, minimizing the need for cessation, and inaccurate information (smoking affects the entire pregnancy, not just the third trimester) are not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: Quitting smoking before getting pregnant helps the person get pregnant more easily and makes the pregnancy safer for the baby. Do not scare or shame the person — offer help and resources instead. Cutting down is better than nothing, but quitting completely is the goal.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching parents about car seat safety for their newborn. Which statement by a parent indicates correct understanding?

options.text: "We can use a secondhand car seat if it looks clean and in good condition."
"The car seat should be installed in the back seat, rear-facing, at a 45-degree angle."
"We should place a thick blanket under the baby in the car seat for comfort."
"The chest clip should be positioned at the baby's abdomen."

rationales.whyCorrect: Car seats should be rear-facing in the back seat at approximately a 45-degree angle to keep the infant's airway open. Secondhand car seats may have been in a crash or be expired. Thick blankets or padding under the baby can compromise harness safety. The chest clip should be at armpit level, not the abdomen.
rationales.eli10: A newborn's car seat must face the back of the car and be at a slight angle (45 degrees) so the baby can breathe easily. Do not use a used car seat — you do not know if it was in a crash. Do not put thick blankets under the baby — they can make the straps not work right. The chest clip goes at armpit level.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a postpartum client who is breastfeeding. The client asks, "How do I know my baby is getting enough milk?" What is the best response?

options.text: "You will be able to feel the milk going into the baby."
"Count wet diapers — six or more wet diapers per day and steady weight gain are good signs."
"The baby will sleep through the night by one week of age."
"If your breasts feel soft, the baby is getting enough."

rationales.whyCorrect: Adequate wet diapers (six or more per day) and steady weight gain are objective indicators of adequate milk intake. Subjective sensations are unreliable. Newborns typically feed every 2 to 3 hours and do not sleep through the night. Breast softness alone does not confirm adequate intake.
rationales.eli10: To know if a breastfed baby is getting enough milk, count wet diapers. Six or more wet diapers a day is a good sign. The baby should also be gaining weight. You cannot feel the milk going in. New babies wake often to feed — that is normal.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing prenatal education about alcohol use during pregnancy. The client asks, "Is it safe to have just one glass of wine on special occasions?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Yes, one glass of wine occasionally is safe during pregnancy."
"No amount of alcohol has been proven safe during pregnancy. Alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders."
"Wine is safe, but hard liquor should be avoided."
"Alcohol is only dangerous in the first trimester."

rationales.whyCorrect: No amount of alcohol has been established as safe during pregnancy. Alcohol crosses the placenta and can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. There is no safe type, no safe amount, and no safe trimester for alcohol consumption during pregnancy.
rationales.eli10: There is no safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy — not even one glass. Alcohol reaches the baby through the placenta and can cause lifelong brain and body problems. This is true for beer, wine, and hard liquor. It is true in every trimester.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about perineal care after a vaginal delivery with an episiotomy. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "Use a peri-bottle with warm water to cleanse the area after voiding or defecating."
"Avoid cleaning the perineal area for the first week to allow healing."
"Take tub baths daily to keep the area clean."
"Apply talcum powder to the episiotomy site to keep it dry."

rationales.whyCorrect: Using a peri-bottle with warm water after voiding or defecating cleanses the perineal area gently and promotes healing. Tub baths are generally avoided initially after delivery. Talcum powder is not recommended. Perineal hygiene should be performed regularly, not avoided.
rationales.eli10: After a vaginal delivery with stitches, use a squirt bottle filled with warm water to clean yourself after using the bathroom. This is gentle and keeps the area clean. Do not take a bath right away. Clean the area every time you use the bathroom — do not skip it.

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling an adolescent about pregnancy prevention. The teen says, "My boyfriend says we don't need protection because he pulls out." What is the nurse's priority teaching point?

options.text: "The withdrawal method is as effective as condoms for preventing pregnancy."
"Withdrawal does not protect against sexually transmitted infections and has a high failure rate for pregnancy prevention."
"You should trust your boyfriend's judgment."
"If you get pregnant, you can always get an abortion."

rationales.whyCorrect: Withdrawal (coitus interruptus) has a high typical-use failure rate for pregnancy prevention and provides no protection against STIs. The nurse must provide accurate, nonjudgmental education. Trusting the boyfriend's judgment or discussing abortion as a backup plan are not appropriate nursing responses.
rationales.eli10: The "pull-out" method does not work well to prevent pregnancy — many people get pregnant this way. It also does not protect against infections like chlamydia, gonorrhea, or HIV. The nurse should explain this without making the teen feel bad.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a postpartum client on day 2 after delivery. The client is tearful, says she feels overwhelmed, and states, "I don't think I can do this." Her vital signs are stable, and she is caring for the baby with encouragement. What is the nurse's best interpretation?

options.text: The client is experiencing postpartum psychosis and needs immediate psychiatric intervention
The client likely has "postpartum blues," a common and usually self-limiting condition
The client has postpartum depression and needs to start an antidepressant immediately
The client is unfit to care for her baby and child protective services should be notified

rationales.whyCorrect: Postpartum blues (baby blues) affect up to 80% of new mothers, usually occurring within the first few days to two weeks after delivery. Symptoms include tearfulness, mood swings, and feeling overwhelmed. The client is still able to care for the baby, and symptoms are mild. Postpartum blues is self-limiting. Postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency with severe symptoms. Postpartum depression involves more persistent and severe symptoms.
rationales.eli10: The "baby blues" happen to most new mothers in the first few days after delivery. Crying, mood swings, and feeling overwhelmed are normal and usually go away on their own within two weeks. If these feelings last longer than two weeks or get worse, it could be postpartum depression and needs treatment. The mother can still care for her baby — she just needs support.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing prenatal teaching about exercise. The client is at 24 weeks of gestation with an uncomplicated pregnancy. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I should avoid all exercise for the rest of my pregnancy."
"I can continue moderate exercise like walking and swimming, but I should avoid activities with a high risk of falling."
"I can continue my CrossFit routine at the same intensity as before pregnancy."
"I should only exercise while lying on my back."

rationales.whyCorrect: Moderate exercise such as walking and swimming is encouraged during uncomplicated pregnancy. Activities with a high risk of falling (horseback riding, skiing) should be avoided. Exercise intensity should be moderate, not at pre-pregnancy high-intensity levels. After the first trimester, lying flat on the back for extended periods should be avoided due to supine hypotensive syndrome.
rationales.eli10: Pregnant people can and should exercise if their pregnancy is healthy. Walking and swimming are great choices. Avoid activities where you could fall, like skiing or horseback riding. Do not exercise lying flat on your back after the first trimester — it can make you feel dizzy.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a group of adolescents about sexually transmitted infections. Which statement by a participant indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Using condoms correctly every time reduces the risk of most STIs."
"Many STIs can be present without causing any symptoms."
"Once you have been treated for an STI, you cannot get it again."
"I should get tested regularly if I am sexually active."

rationales.whyCorrect: Many STIs, such as chlamydia and gonorrhea, can be contracted again after treatment. Having been treated once does not confer immunity. Condoms reduce risk but are not 100% effective. Many STIs are asymptomatic. Regular testing is recommended for sexually active individuals.
rationales.eli10: You can get an STI more than once. Treatment cures the current infection but does not protect you from getting it again in the future. You can have an STI without feeling sick at all. Use condoms, get tested, and talk to partners about testing.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a newborn at 24 hours of life. The mother plans to breastfeed. Which finding warrants further intervention?

options.text: The newborn feeds 8 to 12 times in 24 hours
The newborn has one wet diaper and one stool in the first 24 hours
The newborn has audible swallowing during feeding
The newborn appears content and sleeps between feedings

rationales.whyCorrect: By 24 hours of life, a newborn should have at least one to two wet diapers and one to two stools. One wet diaper and one stool may indicate inadequate intake and warrants further assessment of feeding and hydration. Feeding frequency, audible swallowing, and content behavior between feeds are encouraging signs.
rationales.eli10: In the first day of life, a newborn should wet at least one or two diapers and have a couple of stools. Only one wet diaper in 24 hours might mean the baby is not getting enough milk. The nurse should watch the feedings more closely and check for dehydration.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing preconception counseling to a client with a history of type 1 diabetes. Which teaching point is most important?

options.text: "Your diabetes will not affect a pregnancy at all."
"Achieving good glycemic control before conception reduces the risk of birth defects and pregnancy complications."
"You should stop taking all insulin during pregnancy."
"Women with diabetes cannot have healthy pregnancies."

rationales.whyCorrect: Preconception glycemic control is critical for women with diabetes. Elevated blood glucose during early organ development significantly increases the risk of congenital anomalies. Insulin is safe during pregnancy and is the preferred medication. Women with diabetes can have healthy pregnancies with proper management.
rationales.eli10: If a person with diabetes wants to get pregnant, they should get their blood sugar under good control first. High blood sugar in early pregnancy can cause birth defects. Insulin is safe to use during pregnancy. With good care, people with diabetes can have healthy babies.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about opioid use disorder and pregnancy. The client is on medication-assisted treatment with buprenorphine. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "You must stop buprenorphine immediately because it will harm your baby."
"Continuing buprenorphine during pregnancy is recommended — stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal and risk pregnancy loss."
"Babies born to mothers on buprenorphine never need any special monitoring."
"You should be ashamed of needing medication during pregnancy."

rationales.whyCorrect: Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) with buprenorphine or methadone is the standard of care for opioid use disorder during pregnancy. Abrupt discontinuation can cause fetal withdrawal, miscarriage, or preterm labor. The nurse should provide nonjudgmental, evidence-based education. Newborns exposed to MAT may need monitoring for neonatal abstinence syndrome.
rationales.eli10: If someone is pregnant and taking buprenorphine for opioid addiction, they should keep taking it. Stopping suddenly can cause the baby to go into withdrawal and even cause miscarriage. Buprenorphine is the safest choice. The baby may need extra watching after birth, but staying on the medicine gives the baby the best chance.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching new parents about cord care for their newborn. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: "Submerge the cord stump in water during baths to clean it."
"Keep the cord stump clean and dry, and fold the diaper below the cord."
"Apply alcohol to the cord stump with every diaper change."
"Pull off the cord stump once it starts to loosen."

rationales.whyCorrect: The cord stump should be kept clean and dry. The diaper should be folded below the cord to allow air exposure and prevent contamination. The cord should not be submerged in water. Current guidelines generally recommend dry cord care without routine alcohol application. The cord should be allowed to fall off naturally.
rationales.eli10: Keep the baby's belly button stump clean and dry. Fold the diaper down so it does not cover the stump. Do not put the baby in a tub bath until the stump falls off. Let it fall off on its own — do not pull it.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client at 32 weeks of gestation. The client reports feeling lightheaded when lying flat on the back. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Tell the client this is abnormal and call the provider immediately
Explain that this is supine hypotensive syndrome and recommend lying in a side-lying position
Instruct the client to lie flat and stay still until the feeling passes
Tell the client she needs to go to the emergency department

rationales.whyCorrect: Supine hypotensive syndrome occurs when the gravid uterus compresses the vena cava when the pregnant client lies flat on the back, reducing venous return and causing lightheadedness. The treatment is to position the client in a side-lying position (preferably left lateral). This is a normal physiological response, not an emergency when positional change resolves symptoms.
rationales.eli10: When a pregnant person lies flat on their back, the heavy uterus can press on a big vein. This slows blood return to the heart and makes them feel dizzy. The fix is simple: lie on your side instead. This is common and not an emergency if changing position helps.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about postpartum depression. Which statement indicates the client understands when to seek help?

options.text: "Feeling sad or anxious for more than two weeks after delivery means I should talk to my provider."
"Postpartum depression will go away on its own, so I should just wait it out."
"Only women with a history of depression get postpartum depression."
"If I have postpartum depression, it means I am a bad mother."

rationales.whyCorrect: Postpartum depression is characterized by persistent symptoms lasting more than two weeks. It requires professional evaluation and treatment — it does not typically resolve without intervention. It can affect anyone, not only those with a history of depression. Having postpartum depression does not make someone a bad mother — it is a medical condition.
rationales.eli10: Feeling sad for a few days after having a baby is normal (baby blues). But if sadness, anxiety, or hopelessness lasts more than two weeks, it could be postpartum depression. This needs treatment — it does not usually go away on its own. It is a medical condition, not a sign of being a bad parent.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing discharge teaching to a client after a cesarean birth. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I should avoid lifting anything heavier than my baby for the first few weeks."
"I will call my provider if I notice redness, drainage, or separation at my incision."
"I can start doing sit-ups to strengthen my abdominal muscles right away."
"I will use a pillow to splint my incision when I cough or sneeze."

rationales.whyCorrect: After cesarean birth, abdominal exercises like sit-ups should be avoided for at least 6 weeks or until cleared by the provider. Resuming strenuous core exercises too early can compromise incision healing. The other statements reflect correct understanding of post-cesarean precautions.
rationales.eli10: After a C-section, do not do sit-ups or heavy exercise until the doctor says it is okay — usually at the 6-week check-up. The incision needs time to heal. Lifting only the baby, watching for infection signs, and splinting the incision during coughing are all correct.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about effective breastfeeding technique. Which observation indicates the baby is latched correctly?

options.text: The baby's cheeks are dimpled inward with each suck
Only the nipple — not the areola — is in the baby's mouth
The baby's mouth covers a large portion of the areola, lips are flanged outward, and swallowing is audible
A clicking sound is heard with each suck

rationales.whyCorrect: A correct latch includes the baby's mouth covering a large portion of the areola (not just the nipple), lips flanged outward like a fish, and audible swallowing. Dimpled cheeks, only the nipple in the mouth, and clicking sounds indicate a poor latch that needs correction.
rationales.eli10: A good latch means the baby has more than just the nipple in their mouth — they have a big mouthful of breast. The lips should turn outward. You should hear the baby swallowing. If the cheeks dimple in or you hear clicking, the latch is not right and needs to be fixed.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client who is 2 days postpartum. The client's fundus is firm and at the level of the umbilicus. The client is breastfeeding. The nurse notes lochia rubra with small clots. What action should the nurse take?

options.text: Massage the fundus vigorously until it is below the umbilicus
Document these as normal postpartum findings
Notify the provider immediately
Prepare the client for a dilation and curettage procedure

rationales.whyCorrect: At 2 days postpartum, the fundus is expected to be firm and at the level of the umbilicus. Lochia rubra (red lochia) is normal for the first 3 to 4 days. Small clots are also expected. These are all normal assessment findings that should be documented. No intervention is required.
rationales.eli10: Two days after delivery, the top of the uterus should feel firm and be at the level of the belly button. Bright red bleeding (lochia rubra) is normal for the first few days. Small clots are also normal. The nurse just needs to document these findings — nothing is wrong.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a prenatal class about the signs of preterm labor. Which statement by a participant indicates understanding?

options.text: "Irregular contractions that go away with rest are a sign of preterm labor."
"I should call my provider if I have regular contractions, low back pain, pelvic pressure, or a change in vaginal discharge before 37 weeks."
"Preterm labor only happens to women who have had it before."
"I will know I am in preterm labor because my water will always break dramatically."

rationales.whyCorrect: Signs of preterm labor include regular contractions, low back pain, pelvic pressure, and changes in vaginal discharge before 37 weeks. Any of these warrant immediate notification of the provider. Contractions that go away with rest are Braxton Hicks, not preterm labor. Preterm labor can happen to anyone.
rationales.eli10: If contractions come at regular times, if there is low back pain or pelvic pressure, or if vaginal discharge changes before 37 weeks — call the doctor right away. Preterm labor can happen in any pregnancy. The water does not always break — sometimes the signs are more subtle.

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a client about tobacco cessation. The client says, "I've tried to quit so many times. I just can't do it." Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: "You just need more willpower."
"It sounds like you have been working hard at this. Many people need several attempts before quitting successfully — let's look at what you have tried and what might help this time."
"If you really cared about your health, you would find a way."
"Smoking is not that harmful anyway."

rationales.whyCorrect: The most therapeutic response acknowledges the client's effort, normalizes the difficulty of tobacco cessation, and offers collaborative problem-solving. Shaming, blaming, or minimizing the health risks are not therapeutic and damage the nurse-client relationship.
rationales.eli10: Most people try to quit smoking several times before they succeed. That is normal. The nurse should say: "You have been trying hard. Let's look at what you have tried and figure out a new plan together." Never shame someone for struggling to quit.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing education about newborn screening tests. A parent asks, "Why does my baby need a heel stick before we leave the hospital?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "We test the baby's blood sugar because all newborns have diabetes."
"The newborn screen checks for rare but serious conditions that can be treated early to prevent disability or death."
"It is optional and not really necessary."
"We do it on all babies so the hospital can collect data for research."

rationales.whyCorrect: Newborn screening (the "heel stick" or dried blood spot test) screens for a panel of rare genetic and metabolic conditions including phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, and others. Early detection allows treatment that can prevent severe disability or death. It is not optional in most states — it is standard of care.
rationales.eli10: Before a baby leaves the hospital, a few drops of blood are taken from the heel. This tests for rare diseases that do not show symptoms right away but can cause serious problems if not treated early. Finding these problems early can save the baby's life or prevent brain damage.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a pregnant client about the Tdap vaccine. The client asks why it is recommended during every pregnancy. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: "The vaccine protects you from getting pertussis from your baby."
"The Tdap vaccine is given during pregnancy so that maternal antibodies pass to the baby, protecting the newborn from pertussis until they can be vaccinated."
"It has no benefit to the baby — it is just for your own protection."
"It prevents the baby from getting all childhood diseases."

rationales.whyCorrect: Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy (preferably between 27 and 36 weeks) so that maternal pertussis antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn until they begin their own vaccination series at 2 months. Newborns are highly vulnerable to pertussis.
rationales.eli10: The whooping cough (Tdap) shot is given during every pregnancy. The mother's body makes antibodies that cross the placenta to the baby. This protects the newborn from whooping cough until the baby is old enough to get their own shots. Whooping cough can be deadly for newborns.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a parent about preventing sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Which recommendation should the nurse include?

options.text: Place the baby on the stomach to sleep
Use a firm sleep surface, place the baby on the back, and avoid soft bedding in the crib
Place the baby to sleep with a pacifier attached to a string around the neck
Keep the room very warm and cover the baby with a heavy blanket
