questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating a client's understanding of coping strategies for anxiety. Which statement by the client indicates effective learning?

options.text: "When I feel anxious, I will drink a few glasses of wine to relax."
"When I feel anxiety building, I will practice deep breathing exercises and go for a short walk before the anxiety becomes overwhelming."
"I will avoid all situations that make me anxious."
"Anxiety is just in my head — I can ignore it until it goes away."

rationales.whyCorrect: Effective coping involves intervening early before anxiety escalates, using healthy strategies such as deep breathing and physical activity. Using alcohol is a maladaptive coping mechanism. Avoidance reinforces anxiety over time. Ignoring anxiety does not address it and can lead to worsening symptoms.
rationales.eli10: The best way to handle anxiety is to catch it early. Deep breathing and a short walk can stop anxiety before it spirals. Using alcohol to cope makes things worse. Avoiding anxiety-provoking situations makes fear stronger over time. Face it early with healthy tools.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching an older adult client about preventing falls at home. Which recommendation should the nurse include?

options.text: Keep rooms dimly lit to promote relaxation
Remove throw rugs, install grab bars, and ensure adequate lighting
Wear loose-fitting slippers for comfort
Wax floors regularly for a clean appearance

rationales.whyCorrect: Fall prevention in older adults includes removing tripping hazards (throw rugs), installing grab bars in bathrooms, and ensuring adequate lighting. Dim lighting increases fall risk. Loose slippers and waxed floors are fall hazards.
rationales.eli10: To prevent falls, take away throw rugs — they slide and trip people. Put grab bars by the toilet and in the shower. Make sure rooms are bright enough to see clearly. Wear non-slip shoes or slippers. Do not wax floors — they become slippery.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse, "I feel like I am having a heart attack — my heart is pounding and I can't catch my breath." The client is diaphoretic and tremulous. Vital signs are normal. The client has a history of panic disorder. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Activate the cardiac emergency response team
Stay with the client, reassure them, and coach slow breathing
Leave the client alone to self-soothe
Tell the client: "It's just anxiety — you are fine."

rationales.whyCorrect: The client's symptoms match panic disorder, and vital signs are normal. The priority is to stay with the client, provide reassurance, and coach slow breathing to reduce hyperventilation. Activating the cardiac team or leaving the client alone is inappropriate. Telling the client "it's just anxiety" dismisses their very real experience.
rationales.eli10: A panic attack feels exactly like a heart attack to the person having it. Stay with them — do not leave. Use a calm voice. Coach slow breathing. Even though their vitals are normal, their fear is real. Your presence is what helps most.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing anticipatory guidance to parents of a 4-year-old. Which statement by a parent indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will make sure my child wears a helmet when riding a tricycle."
"I can leave my child in the bathtub alone for a few minutes while I answer the phone."
"I will teach my child to stop at the curb before crossing the street."
"I keep cleaning supplies in a locked cabinet."

rationales.whyCorrect: A 4-year-old should never be left alone in the bathtub — drowning can occur silently in seconds. Helmet use, street safety, and locked cabinets are all appropriate safety measures. The nurse must correct this misconception.
rationales.eli10: Never leave a young child alone in the bath — not even for a minute to grab a towel or answer the phone. A child can drown in just an inch of water, silently and fast. Always stay within arm's reach.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client newly diagnosed with a chronic illness. The client says, "I'll never be able to manage this. My life is over." Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: "Don't be dramatic — many people live full lives with this condition."
"You are right — your life will never be the same."
"This diagnosis is a lot to take in. What feels most overwhelming to you right now?"
"Just take it one day at a time and you'll be fine."

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse should acknowledge the difficulty of the diagnosis and use an open-ended question to explore the client's specific concerns. Dismissing the client's feelings ("don't be dramatic"), agreeing with catastrophic thinking, or using false reassurance ("you'll be fine") are not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: When someone gets scary health news, do not say "don't be dramatic" or "you'll be fine." Those words shut down the conversation. Instead, say: "This is a lot to process. What part feels the hardest right now?" Then listen.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching an adolescent about the risks of tanning beds. Which statement by the adolescent indicates understanding?

options.text: "Tanning beds are safe because they only use UVB rays."
"Tanning beds increase the risk of skin cancer, including melanoma."
"A base tan from a tanning bed protects me from sunburn."
"As long as I don't burn, tanning beds are not harmful."

rationales.whyCorrect: Tanning beds emit UV radiation that increases the risk of all skin cancers, including melanoma. A "base tan" is a sign of skin damage and provides minimal protection. Any tanning bed use is harmful, not just burning.
rationales.eli10: Tanning beds are not safe — they use UV rays that damage skin and cause cancer. There is no such thing as a "safe tan." A tan is visible skin damage. The only safe tan comes from a bottle.

questions.stem: A client with major depressive disorder has been on an antidepressant for two weeks. The client says, "I still feel terrible. This medication isn't working." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You are right — if it hasn't worked by now, it probably won't."
"Antidepressants often take four to six weeks to reach full effect. Let's talk about what small changes you have noticed."
"You just need to be more patient."
"I will ask the doctor to double your dose immediately."

rationales.whyCorrect: Antidepressants typically take four to six weeks to reach full therapeutic effect. The nurse should provide realistic expectations while encouraging the client to notice small improvements. Dismissing or doubling the dose prematurely are not appropriate.
rationales.eli10: Depression medicine does not work overnight. It takes four to six weeks to feel the full effect. That is like waiting for a seed to grow into a plant — it needs time. The nurse should help the client notice tiny improvements while waiting.

questions.stem: A nurse is performing a home safety assessment for a family with a newborn. Which finding requires intervention?

options.text: The crib is placed away from windows and blinds
A crib bumper pad is installed to protect the baby
The smoke detectors are working and have fresh batteries
The water heater is set to 120°F or lower

rationales.whyCorrect: Crib bumper pads are a suffocation hazard and are not recommended for safe infant sleep. The crib away from windows (cord strangulation risk), working smoke detectors, and water heater set to 120°F or lower (scald prevention) are all appropriate safety measures.
rationales.eli10: Crib bumpers are dangerous — babies can suffocate against them. Do not use them. The crib should be bare: just a firm mattress with a fitted sheet. No bumpers, pillows, blankets, or stuffed animals.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client who is experiencing domestic violence. The client says, "I can't leave — I have nowhere to go." Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.text: "You need to leave immediately for your safety."
"Tell me about your concerns. Let's talk about resources and options available to you when you feel ready."
"If you stay, it's your own fault when he hurts you again."
"I'll call the police and have him arrested."

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse should explore the client's concerns without pressure and offer information about resources. Demanding the client leave, blaming the victim, or taking unilateral action (calling police without consent, unless legally required) can increase danger and disempower the client.
rationales.eli10: Do not tell an abuse victim "just leave." It is not that simple — leaving can be dangerous and the person may have no money or safe place. Instead, say: "Tell me your worries. Let me share resources for when you are ready." Give options, not orders.

questions.stem: A school nurse is teaching elementary students about nutrition. Which statement by a student indicates understanding?

options.text: "I should eat candy for energy before a test."
"I should eat a variety of colorful fruits and vegetables every day."
"Skipping breakfast helps me stay focused at school."
"Soda is better than water because it tastes good."

rationales.whyCorrect: Eating a variety of colorful fruits and vegetables provides essential vitamins, minerals, and fiber. Candy provides empty calories. Skipping breakfast impairs concentration. Soda is high in sugar and lacks nutritional value.
rationales.eli10: Eat a rainbow of fruits and vegetables every day. Different colors mean different vitamins. Candy and soda give a quick sugar rush then a crash. Breakfast helps your brain work at school. Eat real food, not junk.

questions.stem: A client is admitted to the psychiatric unit with suicidal ideation. The client asks the nurse, "Can I go outside for a walk by myself?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Of course — fresh air will do you good."
"Right now, for your safety, a staff member will accompany you whenever you leave the unit. Let's take a walk together."
"No — you are not allowed outside until you are discharged."
"If you promise not to hurt yourself, you can go alone."

rationales.whyCorrect: A client with suicidal ideation requires close monitoring. The nurse should explain the safety rationale and offer to accompany the client, maintaining therapeutic presence while ensuring safety. Allowing unsupervised off-unit time or relying on promises are unsafe.
rationales.eli10: A suicidal patient cannot go outside alone — it is not safe. But instead of just saying "no," say: "For safety, a staff member goes with you. Let's take a walk together right now." This keeps them safe while still getting fresh air.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with hypertension about the DASH diet. Which food choice indicates the client understands the teaching?

options.text: A ham and cheese sandwich with potato chips
Grilled salmon with steamed vegetables and brown rice
Fried chicken with macaroni and cheese
Canned soup with saltine crackers

rationales.whyCorrect: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean protein, and low sodium. Grilled salmon with vegetables and brown rice aligns with these principles. Ham, chips, fried foods, and canned soup are high in sodium.
rationales.eli10: The DASH diet for high blood pressure means: lots of fruits and veggies, whole grains, and lean meats like fish. Grilled salmon with veggies and brown rice is a perfect DASH meal. Ham, chips, fried food, and canned soup have too much salt.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who is terminally ill and has requested no further aggressive treatment. The client's family insists that "everything" be done. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Follow the family's wishes since the client is too sick to decide
Advocate for the client's previously stated wishes and facilitate a family meeting with the healthcare team
Tell the family their wishes do not matter
Ignore the conflict and continue with the current plan without discussion

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse's primary duty is to advocate for the client's autonomy and previously stated wishes. Facilitating a family meeting allows for communication, education, and support while upholding the client's rights. Overriding the client's decisions or dismissing the family is not appropriate.
rationales.eli10: If a dying patient said "no more aggressive treatment," the nurse must honor that — even if the family disagrees. The patient's voice matters most. Set up a meeting with the family and doctors to explain the patient's wishes and answer questions.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of middle-aged adults about colorectal cancer screening. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I only need screening if I have rectal bleeding."
"Screening should begin at age 45 for average-risk adults."
"A colonoscopy is the same as a prostate exam."
"Once I have one normal colonoscopy, I never need another."

rationales.whyCorrect: Colorectal cancer screening should begin at age 45 for average-risk adults. Screening is for asymptomatic individuals — waiting for bleeding means waiting for symptoms. A colonoscopy is not a prostate exam. Repeat screening is needed based on findings and risk.
rationales.eli10: Colon cancer screening starts at age 45 — even if you feel fine. You do not wait for symptoms. A colonoscopy looks at the colon with a camera. You need more than one in your lifetime. Screening finds problems before they become cancer.

questions.stem: A nurse is working with a client who has social anxiety disorder. The client says, "I can't go to the group activity — everyone will stare at me." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You are right — it's better if you stay in your room."
"No one will stare at you — you're being paranoid."
"It sounds like the thought of being around others is very frightening. Would it help if we walked in together and sat near the door?"
"If you don't participate, you won't get better."

rationales.whyCorrect: For social anxiety, graded exposure with support is therapeutic. Offering to accompany the client and providing an "escape plan" (sitting near the door) reduces anxiety while encouraging participation. Forcing participation, dismissing the fear, or reinforcing avoidance are not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: Someone with social anxiety is terrified of being watched. Do not force them or call them paranoid. Say: "I know this is scary. What if we go in together and sit near the door so you can leave if it gets too much?" Small, supported steps build confidence.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a 3-month-old infant. The parent asks, "When should my baby start getting teeth?" Which response is most accurate?

options.text: "All babies get their first tooth by 3 months."
"Most infants get their first tooth around 6 months, but the range varies from 4 to 12 months."
"If your baby doesn't have teeth by 3 months, something is wrong."
"Teeth do not come in until after the first birthday."

rationales.whyCorrect: The first tooth typically erupts around 6 months, but normal variation ranges from 4 to 12 months. Some infants are born with teeth; others do not get them until after their first birthday. Both extremes can be normal.
rationales.eli10: Most babies get their first tooth around 6 months old. But some get teeth as early as 4 months, and some not until after their first birthday. Both can be totally normal. Do not worry if your 3-month-old does not have teeth yet.

questions.stem: A client is being discharged after treatment for alcohol use disorder. The client asks, "How will I handle cravings when I get home?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You just need to have more willpower."
"Let's identify your triggers and develop a plan. We can discuss coping strategies, support groups, and medications that can help."
"Avoid everyone you know and stay inside."
"One drink won't hurt if the craving gets too strong."

rationales.whyCorrect: Relapse prevention involves identifying triggers, developing coping strategies, engaging support systems, and considering medication options. Telling the client to use willpower, isolate, or that "one drink won't hurt" are dangerous and not evidence-based.
rationales.eli10: Before leaving the hospital, help the patient make a plan for cravings. What are their triggers? Who can they call? What coping skills work? There are also medicines that reduce cravings. Willpower alone is not enough — everyone needs a plan.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about testicular self-examination. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: "I should perform the exam once every five years."
"The best time is after a warm bath or shower, using gentle rolling motions."
"Lumps are only concerning if they are painful."
"Testicular self-exams are only for men who are sexually active."

rationales.whyCorrect: Testicular self-examination should be performed monthly after a warm bath or shower when the scrotum is relaxed. Use gentle rolling motions. Lumps should be reported whether painful or not. All males from adolescence onward should perform self-exams.
rationales.eli10: Check your testicles once a month. The best time is after a warm shower — the skin is relaxed and it is easier to feel. Roll each testicle gently between your fingers. Any lump — painful or not — needs a doctor's check. Start doing this as a teenager.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who has just learned that a close family member died unexpectedly. The client is staring blankly and not responding. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Leave the client alone to process the news
Stay with the client, use silence, and offer physical presence without demanding a response
Ask detailed questions about funeral arrangements
Tell the client they need to "snap out of it"

rationales.whyCorrect: Shock is a common initial reaction to sudden loss. The client may be unable to process or respond. The nurse should stay with the client, use silence, and offer presence. Leaving the client alone, demanding practical decisions, or telling them to "snap out of it" are harmful.
rationales.eli10: When someone is in shock after terrible news, they may just stare and not respond. Do not leave them alone. Just sit with them. You do not need to say anything. Your quiet presence is enough. They will talk when they are ready.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a new mother about postpartum warning signs. Which statement by the mother indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I should call my provider if I have thoughts of hurting myself or the baby."
"A headache that doesn't go away with Tylenol could be a sign of a problem."
"Bright red bleeding that increases instead of decreases is not normal."
"Foul-smelling vaginal discharge is normal and expected after delivery."

rationales.whyCorrect: Foul-smelling vaginal discharge after delivery is a sign of infection (endometritis) and should be reported immediately. Thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby, persistent headache, and increased bright red bleeding are all valid warning signs that the client correctly identified.
rationales.eli10: After delivery, vaginal discharge should not smell bad. A foul smell means infection — call the doctor. Thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby, bad headaches that do not go away, and bleeding that gets heavier instead of lighter are all reasons to call immediately.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client with generalized anxiety disorder. The client is worried about an upcoming medical test. Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "Stop worrying — the test is routine."
"What specifically about the test is worrying you?"
"If you just don't think about it, you'll feel better."
"Worrying only makes things worse."

rationales.whyCorrect: Focusing on specifics helps the client articulate the concern and moves from generalized anxiety to a concrete topic that can be addressed. Telling the client to stop worrying, minimizing the concern, or giving advice is not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: When a patient is worrying about a test, do not say "stop worrying." Ask: "What exactly about the test scares you?" This helps them think clearly instead of just feeling overwhelmed. Then you can address each specific fear.

questions.stem: A nurse is conducting a health screening for a 65-year-old client. The client asks, "Do I still need vaccines at my age?" Which vaccines should the nurse recommend?

options.text: No vaccines are needed after age 65
Influenza annually, Tdap or Td booster every 10 years, shingles vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine
Only the childhood vaccine series repeated
Only the COVID-19 vaccine

rationales.whyCorrect: Older adults need: annual influenza vaccine, Tdap or Td booster every 10 years, shingles vaccine (age 50+), and pneumococcal vaccine (age 65+). Immunization needs continue throughout life — they do not end in childhood.
rationales.eli10: Older adults still need vaccines. Get a flu shot every year. Get a tetanus booster every 10 years. Get the shingles vaccine — shingles is very painful and common in older adults. Get the pneumonia vaccine. Vaccines are not just for kids.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse, "Sometimes I drink a whole bottle of wine by myself after work, but I'm not an alcoholic — I have a job and a family." What is the nurse's most appropriate response?

options.text: "You are right — functioning people cannot be alcoholics."
"Alcohol use disorder can affect anyone regardless of job or family status. Drinking an entire bottle of wine alone raises concerns. Can we talk more about your drinking?"
"Everyone needs a way to unwind."
"I will document that you are an alcoholic."

rationales.whyCorrect: Alcohol use disorder can affect individuals regardless of socioeconomic status or family situation — this is known as "high-functioning." Drinking an entire bottle of wine alone regularly indicates risky drinking. Labeling the client an alcoholic is not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: You can have a job, a family, and still have a drinking problem. This is called high-functioning. Drinking a whole bottle of wine alone after work regularly is not healthy. The nurse should ask caring questions, not slap on a label.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching parents about promoting language development in their 18-month-old. Which activity does the nurse recommend?

options.text: "Limit talking to your child so they learn to speak independently."
"Read to your child daily, name objects, and respond to their attempts to communicate."
"Correct every word your child mispronounces immediately."
"Screen time is the best way to teach language skills."

rationales.whyCorrect: Reading to children daily, naming objects in the environment, and responding to communication attempts are evidence-based strategies to promote language development. Limiting talk, overcorrecting, and screen time are not recommended.
rationales.eli10: To help a toddler learn to talk, read to them every day. Point at things and name them: "Look — a dog!" Respond when they try to talk — even if you cannot understand the words. Do not correct every mistake. Just keep the conversation going.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who is Muslim and at end of life. The family asks that the client's body be turned toward Mecca. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "We do not accommodate religious requests in the hospital."
"I will work with the team to position your loved one as you wish. Please tell me about any other practices that are important to you."
"That is not necessary — the direction of the body doesn't matter after death."
"That can only be done after the body is released to the funeral home."

rationales.whyCorrect: Cultural and religious practices at end of life should be honored whenever possible. The nurse should collaborate with the team to accommodate the request and invite the family to share other important practices. Dismissing or delaying the request is not culturally competent care.
rationales.eli10: If a dying Muslim patient's family asks to position the body toward Mecca, make it happen. Ask: "Tell me what else is important to you." These rituals matter deeply. The hospital should accommodate religious practices at the end of life.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an adolescent who appears withdrawn, has declining grades, and has lost interest in activities they previously enjoyed. The parent says, "It's just a phase." What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Agree with the parent and take no further action
Assess the adolescent privately for depression, including asking about suicidal thoughts
Tell the parent they are wrong and should be more concerned
Recommend the adolescent join more extracurricular activities

rationales.whyCorrect: Withdrawal, declining grades, and loss of interest in activities (anhedonia) are warning signs of depression in adolescents — not just a "phase." The nurse must assess privately, including screening for suicidal ideation. Dismissing the signs or prescribing activities without assessment is inappropriate.
rationales.eli10: A teen who stops caring about things they used to love, pulls away from friends, and has falling grades is not "just going through a phase." These are signs of depression. The nurse must talk to them alone and ask about suicidal thoughts. Take it seriously.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing education about sleep hygiene. Which recommendation should the nurse include?

options.text: "Use your phone or tablet in bed to help you fall asleep."
"Keep a consistent sleep schedule, avoid caffeine in the evening, and keep the bedroom dark and cool."
"Exercise vigorously right before bedtime to tire yourself out."
"Drink a glass of wine before bed to help you sleep."

rationales.whyCorrect: Good sleep hygiene includes a consistent sleep-wake schedule, avoiding caffeine in the evening, and keeping the bedroom dark, cool, and quiet. Screen time before bed, vigorous exercise near bedtime, and alcohol disrupt sleep quality.
rationales.eli10: For better sleep: go to bed and wake up at the same time every day — even on weekends. No caffeine after lunch. Keep your bedroom dark and cool. Put your phone away an hour before bed. Do not exercise hard right before sleep. No alcohol — it ruins sleep quality.

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder says to the nurse, "I'm going to kill myself if you don't let me call my mother right now." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Go ahead — I don't believe you."
"I hear that you are very upset. I take any statement about suicide seriously. Let's talk about what is making you feel this way right now."
"Fine, I'll let you call — just don't hurt yourself."
"Threatening suicide is manipulative. Stop it."

rationales.whyCorrect: Any statement about suicide must be taken seriously, even if the nurse suspects it may be manipulative. The nurse should acknowledge the distress and assess the underlying feelings. Dismissing, giving in to demands without therapeutic exploration, or accusing the client of manipulation is not appropriate.
rationales.eli10: When a patient threatens suicide — even if you think they are trying to get something — take it seriously every single time. Say: "I hear that you are very upset. I take what you said seriously. Let's talk about what is really going on." Never ignore suicide threats.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about breast cancer screening. The client is 40 years old with no family history. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: "You do not need mammograms until age 50."
"Guidelines recommend discussing mammography with your provider starting at age 40 and making a shared decision about when to begin screening."
"You need a mammogram every month starting now."
"Breast self-exams are all you need — no imaging is required."

rationales.whyCorrect: Guidelines recommend that women at average risk discuss mammography with their provider starting at age 40. Shared decision-making considers individual values and risk. Mammography is not done monthly. Breast self-awareness is important, but it does not replace mammography.
rationales.eli10: At age 40, talk with your doctor about when to start mammograms. It is not a one-size-fits-all answer. You and your doctor decide together based on your health and preferences. Mammograms are done every 1 to 2 years — not every month. Doing self-exams is good, but you still need mammograms.

questions.stem: A client in the psychiatric unit tells the nurse, "The CIA put a tracking device in my tooth filling." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "That is ridiculous — the CIA does not track people through dental fillings."
"That must feel very frightening. I don't share that belief, but I want to understand how it is affecting you."
"You are right — we should call the police."
"Why would the CIA be interested in you?"

rationales.whyCorrect: Do not argue with a delusion, but do not reinforce it. Acknowledge the client's emotional experience without agreeing with the false belief, then explore the impact. Arguing, reinforcing, or asking "why" are not therapeutic approaches.
rationales.eli10: When a patient says something that is not real (like a tracking device in their tooth), do not argue. Do not pretend you believe it either. Say: "That sounds terrifying. I do not share that belief, but I want to understand how it affects you." Focus on the feeling, not the fact.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning a community health program to increase physical activity among older adults. Which activity is most appropriate?

options.text: High-intensity interval training classes
Low-impact activities such as chair yoga, walking clubs, and tai chi
Competitive contact sports leagues
Marathon training programs

rationales.whyCorrect: Low-impact activities such as chair yoga, walking clubs, and tai chi are appropriate for older adults because they improve strength, balance, and cardiovascular health while minimizing injury risk. High-intensity, competitive, or extreme endurance activities are not appropriate for most older adults.
rationales.eli10: For older adults, choose gentle movement. Chair yoga, walking groups, and tai chi are great choices. They build strength and balance without risking injury. No marathons or competitive sports — keep it low-impact and fun.

questions.stem: A client is being discharged after treatment for depression. The client says, "I'm afraid the bad feelings will come back." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "They probably will — depression never really goes away."
"Recovery isn't always a straight line. Let's review your warning signs and your plan for what to do if you start feeling worse."
"You'll be fine — just think positive."
"If you feel bad again, it means treatment has failed."

rationales.whyCorrect: Depression recovery often involves setbacks. The nurse should normalize this and prepare the client with a relapse prevention plan including warning signs and coping strategies. Hopeless predictions, false reassurance, or suggesting treatment has failed are not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: Recovery from depression has ups and downs — that is normal. Before the patient leaves, make a plan: "What are your early warning signs? Who will you call? What will you do if you start feeling worse?" Having a plan reduces fear and increases confidence.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an older adult for elder abuse. Which finding is most concerning?

options.text: The client has reading glasses
The client has unexplained bruises in various stages of healing and appears fearful of the caregiver
The client takes multiple medications for chronic conditions
The client uses a walker for ambulation

rationales.whyCorrect: Unexplained bruises in various stages of healing combined with fear of the caregiver are classic signs of physical elder abuse. Reading glasses, multiple medications (polypharmacy), and walker use are common in older adults and not inherently concerning.
rationales.eli10: Bruises that cannot be explained, especially in different colors (some fresh, some old), plus a patient who seems scared of their caregiver — that is a major red flag for abuse. Report it. Reading glasses, using a walker, and taking several medicines are normal for older adults.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Which intervention is an example of primary prevention?

options.text: Taking a daily aspirin after a heart attack
Attending cardiac rehabilitation after bypass surgery
Following a heart-healthy diet and exercising regularly to prevent heart disease
Having a stress test to check for coronary artery disease

rationales.whyCorrect: Primary prevention prevents disease from occurring. Heart-healthy diet and exercise prevent cardiovascular disease before it starts. Aspirin after heart attack and cardiac rehab are tertiary. Stress test is secondary (screening).
rationales.eli10: Primary prevention stops disease before it ever happens. Eating well and exercising to keep your heart healthy is primary prevention — you are preventing heart disease. Taking aspirin after a heart attack is tertiary — you already have the disease. Stress tests are secondary — they look for disease.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who is crying and says, "I just got diagnosed with HIV. I feel so dirty and ashamed." What is the nurse's most therapeutic response?

options.text: "You should have been more careful."
"An HIV diagnosis is not a reflection of your worth as a person. This is a manageable medical condition. I am here to support you."
"At least there are medications now."
"How did you get it?"

rationales.whyCorrect: HIV carries significant stigma. The nurse must separate the diagnosis from the person's worth and emphasize that HIV is a manageable chronic condition. Blaming, using platitudes, or asking "how" is judgmental and not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: When someone gets diagnosed with HIV, they often feel ashamed. The nurse should say: "This does not change who you are as a person. HIV is a manageable medical condition now. I am here for you." Do not ask how they got it. Do not blame. Just support.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing teaching about infant safety. The parent asks, "When can I turn my baby's car seat forward-facing?" Which response is correct?

options.text: "As soon as the baby turns one year old."
"Keep the baby rear-facing as long as possible — at least until age 2, and longer if the car seat's height and weight limits allow."
"Forward-facing is fine from birth if it is in the back seat."
"Once the baby weighs 15 pounds, you can switch."

rationales.whyCorrect: Current best practice is to keep children rear-facing as long as possible — at minimum until age 2, but longer if the car seat's limits allow. Rear-facing provides superior protection for the head, neck, and spine. Forward-facing at age 1 is outdated guidance.
rationales.eli10: Keep your child rear-facing as long as you can — at least until age 2, and even longer if the car seat allows. Rear-facing protects the head, neck, and spine in a crash much better than forward-facing. Do not rush to turn them around.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who is experiencing acute grief after the death of a child. The client says, "I hear my child's voice at night." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "You need to see a psychiatrist — hearing voices is serious."
"It's not uncommon for grieving parents to think they hear their child. Can you tell me more about what that experience is like for you?"
"Your child is dead — you cannot hear their voice."
"You are hallucinating and need medication."

rationales.whyCorrect: Sensory experiences of the deceased (hearing their voice, feeling their presence) are common in normal grief and are not necessarily hallucinations or psychosis. The nurse should normalize this experience and invite the client to share. Pathologizing grief is not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: After losing a child, some parents hear the child's voice or feel their presence. This is a normal part of grief — it is not "going crazy." The nurse should say: "That is actually common in grief. Tell me about it." Do not say they need a psychiatrist.

questions.stem: A community health nurse is planning an immunization campaign. Which population should receive the herpes zoster (shingles) vaccine according to current guidelines?

options.text: Newborns
Adolescents aged 11 to 12
Adults aged 50 and older
All adults regardless of age

rationales.whyCorrect: The shingles vaccine is recommended for adults aged 50 and older, even if they have had shingles before or received the older vaccine. Shingles is not a childhood disease — it is reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. It is not given to children or adolescents.
rationales.eli10: The shingles vaccine is for adults 50 and older. Shingles is the chickenpox virus waking up in your body years later — it causes a very painful rash. Even if you had shingles before, you should still get the vaccine. It is not for kids or young adults.

questions.stem: A nurse is conducting a group therapy session. One client makes a sarcastic comment about another client's weight. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Ignore the comment to avoid conflict
Address the behavior calmly: "Comments about other people's bodies are not acceptable in this group. Let's focus on supporting each other."
Ask the targeted client to respond to the comment
End the group session immediately

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse facilitator must maintain a safe, respectful group environment. Addressing the inappropriate behavior calmly but directly sets boundaries while modeling appropriate communication. Ignoring the comment, making the targeted client respond, or ending the session are not appropriate.
rationales.eli10: If someone in group therapy makes a mean comment about another person's body, the nurse must address it right away. Calmly say: "That kind of comment is not okay here. We support each other in this group." Do not ignore it. Protect the safety of the group.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching new parents about safe infant sleep. The parent asks, "Can the baby sleep in our bed with us?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Yes, bed-sharing is recommended for bonding."
"Room-sharing without bed-sharing is recommended for at least the first six months. The baby should sleep in a separate crib or bassinet in your room."
"Bed-sharing is safest when the parents have not been drinking."
"As long as you use pillows around the baby, bed-sharing is safe."

rationales.whyCorrect: Room-sharing (baby in the same room but on a separate sleep surface) is recommended for at least the first 6 months, ideally the first year. Bed-sharing increases the risk of SIDS and accidental suffocation. Pillows around the baby increase suffocation risk.
rationales.eli10: The safest setup: baby sleeps in your room but in their own crib or bassinet — not in your bed. Keep this up for at least 6 months. Sharing a bed increases the risk of the baby suffocating or dying of SIDS. Pillows make it even more dangerous.

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia has been stable on medication for six months. The client says, "I stopped taking my pills last week because I felt fine." What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Respect the client's decision to stop the medication
Explore the reasons for stopping, educate about the risk of relapse, and notify the provider
Tell the client they will be re-hospitalized immediately
Document that the client is noncompliant

rationales.whyCorrect: Medication nonadherence is common in schizophrenia and often leads to relapse. The nurse should explore the reasons (side effects, feeling well, lack of insight), educate about relapse risk, and notify the provider. Respecting the decision without intervention or threatening hospitalization is not therapeutic.
rationales.eli10: When a patient with schizophrenia stops their medicine because they "feel fine," the nurse needs to act. Ask why they stopped — maybe the side effects were bad. Explain that feeling fine means the medicine is working, and stopping could make symptoms come back. Tell the doctor.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing education to an adolescent about the consequences of vaping. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: "Vaping is a safe way to quit smoking."
"Vaping products contain nicotine and other chemicals that can harm brain development and lung health."
"Vaping is just flavored water vapor — it is harmless."
"Vaping only affects older adults."

rationales.whyCorrect: Vaping products contain nicotine — a highly addictive substance that harms adolescent brain development — and other chemicals that damage lungs. Vaping is not a safe alternative to smoking, is not just water vapor, and is not harmless.
rationales.eli10: Vaping is not safe. The liquid has nicotine — the same addictive drug in cigarettes. Nicotine is especially bad for teenage brains. Vaping also has chemicals that can damage lungs. It is not "just water vapor." It is not harmless.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse, "My husband hits me when he drinks, but he's a good man. He always apologizes." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "He sounds like a great husband — everyone makes mistakes."
"Abuse is never okay, even if someone apologizes. You deserve to be safe. Would you like to talk about resources that can help you?"
"You should hit him back."
"If you stay with him, it's your own fault."

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse must clearly state that abuse is never acceptable and offer resources without pressure. Apologizing does not excuse violence. Blaming the victim or suggesting retaliation are harmful responses. The cycle of violence includes a "honeymoon" phase with apologies — this does not mean the abuse will stop.
rationales.eli10: Apologizing after hitting does not make abuse okay. The nurse should say: "Hitting is never okay, no matter what. You deserve to be safe. Can I share some resources?" Do not tell the victim to leave — that could be dangerous. Do not blame. Offer help and let them decide.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client's readiness to learn about diabetes self-management. The client says, "I don't even know what diabetes is." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Hand the client a stack of booklets and pamphlets
Start with basic education about what diabetes is and how it affects the body before teaching self-management skills
Skip education — the client is not ready
Tell the client to Google it

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse must assess the client's baseline knowledge and start education at that level. Handing over materials without context, skipping education, or referring to the internet are not effective teaching strategies. Education must match the learner's readiness and current understanding.
rationales.eli10: If a patient says "I don't even know what diabetes is," start there. Do not hand them a stack of booklets. Do not say "Google it." Start with the basics: "Diabetes means your body has trouble using sugar for energy." Build from the ground up.

questions.stem: A client is pacing in the hallway at 3 AM. The nurse asks what is wrong, and the client says, "I can't turn off my brain. I keep thinking about all the things I did wrong in my life." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You should try harder to stop thinking."
"It sounds like your mind is very busy tonight. Would you like to sit and talk, or would a warm decaffeinated drink help?"
"Everyone has regrets — get over it."
"I'll get you a sleeping pill."

rationales.whyCorrect: Acknowledging the client's racing thoughts and offering choices (talk or a warm, decaffeinated drink) provides support while respecting autonomy. Telling the client to "stop thinking" or "get over it" is dismissive. Immediately offering a sleeping pill without further assessment is not appropriate.
rationales.eli10: When someone's mind is racing at 3 AM, do not say "just stop thinking." That is impossible. Say: "Your mind sounds really busy tonight. Want to talk, or would a warm drink help?" Offer comfort and company. Do not jump to pills.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about type 2 diabetes prevention. The client has prediabetes. Which statement indicates the client understands?

options.text: "Prediabetes always turns into diabetes — there is nothing I can do."
"Losing 5 to 7 percent of my body weight and getting 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week can prevent or delay type 2 diabetes."
"I should cut out all carbohydrates completely."
"I only need to worry about diabetes if I have symptoms."

rationales.whyCorrect: Evidence shows that losing 5 to 7 percent of body weight and getting 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week can reduce the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes by 58 percent. Prediabetes is reversible. Carbohydrates should be managed, not eliminated. Asymptomatic disease still causes damage.
rationales.eli10: Prediabetes means your blood sugar is high but not yet diabetes. You can turn this around. Lose a small amount of weight — just 5 to 7 percent. Walk or exercise for 30 minutes, 5 days a week. These simple changes can prevent diabetes. You do not need to cut out all carbs.

questions.stem: A nurse is admitting a client who is transgender. The client's identification documents have a different name than the name the client uses. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Use only the name on the identification documents
Ask the client: "What name and pronouns do you use?" and document the response for the care team
Avoid using any name to prevent offense
Make a joke to lighten the mood

rationales.whyCorrect: The nurse should ask the client's name and pronouns, not assume based on documentation. This demonstrates respect and cultural competence. Using only legal documents, avoiding names, or making jokes are not acceptable approaches.
rationales.eli10: When a transgender patient's ID has a different name than the one they use, just ask: "What name and pronouns do you use?" Then write it down and share with the team. It is that simple. This shows basic respect. Never joke about it.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who just received a terminal diagnosis. The client's spouse asks, "How long does my husband have?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "He has about six months."
"I wish I could give you an exact answer, but every person's journey is different. The healthcare team can talk with you about what to expect in general terms. I am here to support you both."
"You shouldn't ask that question — it's not helpful."
"He could go at any minute."

rationales.whyCorrect: Prognostication is difficult and imprecise. The nurse should honestly acknowledge uncertainty while offering support and facilitating communication with the healthcare team. Giving specific timelines, scolding the spouse, or making alarming statements are not appropriate.
rationales.eli10: When a family asks "how long," do not guess. Say: "I wish I could tell you exactly, but everyone's journey is different. The doctors can talk with you about what to expect. I am here for you." Honesty about not knowing is better than making up an answer.

questions.stem: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is newly prescribed warfarin. The client also takes several herbal supplements. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Tell the client to continue all supplements — they are natural and safe
Ask the client to list every supplement, educate about potential interactions with warfarin, and recommend the provider review the complete list
Tell the client to stop all supplements immediately without consulting anyone
Document the supplements without further action

rationales.whyCorrect: Warfarin has numerous interactions with herbal supplements (e.g., ginkgo, garlic, St. John's wort, vitamin E). The nurse must identify all supplements and ensure the provider reviews for potential interactions. "Natural" does not mean "safe with prescription medications."
rationales.eli10: Herbal supplements can interact dangerously with blood thinners like warfarin. Just because something is "natural" does not mean it is safe with prescription drugs. The nurse must ask the patient to list every supplement, then have the doctor review the list.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who is withdrawn, has poor eye contact, and speaks in a monotone voice. The client has a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate for the client's social isolation?

options.text: Insist the client attend every group activity on the unit
Spend brief, frequent periods of time with the client, even in silence, to build trust and demonstrate caring
Leave the client alone until they are ready to talk
Tell the client that isolating makes depression worse

rationales.whyCorrect: For a withdrawn, depressed client, brief, frequent contacts — even just sitting silently — communicate caring without overwhelming the client. Forcing group participation, leaving the client alone, or lecturing about isolation are not therapeutic. The client needs connection on their terms.
rationales.eli10: A depressed person who isolates needs gentle connection. Do not force them into groups. Do not leave them alone. Spend short periods of time with them — even 5 minutes of quiet sitting. Say: "I am going to sit with you for a few minutes." Your steady presence shows you care.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to discharge a client after a first psychotic episode. The client's family asks, "What should we watch for at home?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "If the client sleeps a lot, that is a bad sign."

"Watch for early warning signs like changes in sleep, withdrawal from family, suspiciousness, or unusual thoughts. If you notice these, contact the provider early — early intervention can prevent a full relapse."
"You do not need to worry about anything — they are cured."
"If the client acts normally, they are probably faking it."

rationales.whyCorrect: Relapse prevention education includes teaching families to recognize early warning signs (prodromal symptoms) and seek early intervention. Sleep disturbance, withdrawal, suspiciousness, and unusual thoughts can precede a full psychotic episode. Telling families not to worry or accusing the client of faking is harmful.
rationales.eli10: After a first psychotic episode, teach the family what to watch for: changes in sleep, pulling away from family, becoming suspicious, or strange thoughts. Catching these early warning signs and calling the doctor quickly can prevent another full episode. Early action matters.
